Fairness at Fleet Scale

How five principles of distributive justice reshape aircraft routing as the fleet grows past the size of the map — solved to proven optimality with no time budget at all.

The question

Does the choice of principle change how the system performs?

Three families of metric, one answer each. The test is the same every time: across the conditions proven optimal at one fleet size, is the spread between them large enough that a reader could act on it? Unproven cells are excluded throughout — a stopped search pays a worse arrival penalty for having been stopped, which would manufacture exactly the travel-time difference this is looking for.

Congestion

Moves — below the floor

8aircraft spread, at N=30

The conditions do differ in how hard the busiest community is hit. But one condition on its own covers a wider range than that when an incidental parameter moves, so the ordering is not evidence about the principle.

Travel time

Zero in distance, real in timing

0extra hops, every size

Every condition flies the shortest-path floor at every fleet size, and keeps doing so given four extra timesteps of room. The cost is in when aircraft leave: up to 3 aircraft-timesteps of extra departure delay at N=6.

Added noise

Only the objectives clear the floor

3.98dB peak spread, at N=24

Utilitarian halves the summed burden at N=8 — nearly twice the floor, so it is the principle doing it. Among the cap-based conditions the noise differences are smaller than the arbitrary variation.

But how large is a difference?

Most of those differences are below the solver’s own indifference. Equal and Sufficientarian carry no objective; Prioritarian’s evaluates to 0 at every fleet size and horizon solved, so it pins nothing. For all three and the baseline the only quantity being minimised is the arrival penalty — and that optimum is identical at every horizon (22 at N=8, 44 at N=16, 66 at N=24). Move only the horizon, change nothing any of them optimises, and the routing still comes back different. The range one condition covers that way is a floor: a between-condition gap smaller than it is not evidence about the condition.

What the sweep shows

  • 01

    A cap does nothing until the fleet outgrows the map. At N=6 and N=8, Equal, Sufficientarian and the no-fairness baseline return one identical routing — same count matrix at every timestep, same paths. They separate only from N=14.

  • 02

    The condition holding the fewest aircraft over any community is the loudest. At N=24 Equal peaks at 10.00 dB against the baseline’s 7.78, while carrying 9 aircraft over its busiest tile against 13.

  • 03

    Fairness is free in travel time and expensive in compute. Every proven cell flies shortest paths at every fleet size. The cap-based conditions prove out to N=32; the two decibel-valued objectives stop at N=8.

Experiment 1

Congestion: routing under each principle as the fleet grows

Does choosing a fairness principle change where the traffic goes, and does that change with fleet size?

Setup. Six conditions on one instance, eight fleet sizes from N=6 to N=32, unlimited solver budget. Everything except the fairness term is held fixed: same map, same demand, same adjacency, same soft-T arrival tie-break.

Each panel is the same 5×5 map of Austin: tiles shaded by ambient level, the three vertiports ringed, and every aircraft’s path overlaid with line width proportional to the traffic on that leg. Rows are fleet sizes; columns are conditions.

Read it down a column to see one principle respond to a growing fleet, and across a row to see the principles disagree at one fleet size. At N=8 the cap-based columns are indistinguishable from the baseline. By N=32 they are not.

Distance from the no-fairness routing

L1 distance between per-community occupancy vectors, normalised so 0 is the same map and 1 is disjoint. Zero means the principle returned exactly what the solver serves when no principle is chosen.

Experiment 2

Travel time: the cost is real, but it is not distance

How much longer does the fleet fly under each principle than it strictly has to?

Setup. Total fleet hops against the shortest-path floor, and against the no-fairness baseline at the same N. Proven cells only, because a stopped search pays extra arrival time for having been stopped.

Total fleet hops equal the shortest-path floor — and equal the baseline’s — for every proven cell at every fleet size. Average trip length is identical across conditions at each size; it varies with N only because rounding the demand changes which origin–destination pairs are in the mix.

This is a property of the principles, not of a horizon too tight to detour in. Re-solving at N=16 with three extra timesteps leaves Equal, Sufficientarian and Prioritarian proven optimal and still flying 44 fleet hops against a floor of 44. Given room, they decline to use it.

That holds at every cap the tool would plausibly send. It stops holding at the very edge of feasibility: tightening D from 10 to 4 at N=16 makes Equal fly 3 fleet-hops above the floor and Sufficientarian 4, both proven optimal and the only cells in this study where any condition flies further than it has to — and one decibel lower, at D=3, the solver proves no routing exists at all. The detour lives in that single step.

Experiment 3

Added noise: a uniform cap is not a uniform rule

How much noise does each principle create, and which communities carry the worst of it?

Setup. Peak and summed added decibels read off the routing the solver returned, plus utilisation of the capacity each condition’s own cap actually grants a tile at that ambient level.

Because noise adds in energy, a cap on added decibels buys wildly different capacity depending on how loud a community already is. Under D = 10 dB the same number admits 9 simultaneous overflights over a 45 dBA community, 90 over a 55 dBA one and 900 over a 65 dBA one.

So Equal’s disparity cap pushes traffic off the loud tiles the baseline was content to stack aircraft on, and onto quiet ones where four aircraft already add 6.99 dB. Its utilisation of quiet-tile capacity climbs steadily while its loud-tile utilisation never exceeds 0.01 — the cap binds entirely on the quiet.

What the columns mean

Condition
Which of the six payloads was solved — one of the five fairness principles, or Baseline: the same fleet with both caps opened to 30 dB and every objective switched off, i.e. the shortest-time routing the solver returns when no principle has been chosen.
Cap D
The added-noise ceiling in decibels sent to the solver. Equal and Sufficientarian send 10; the other conditions send the wide cap of 30, which no tile on this map can reach, so it binds on nothing.
Tier utilisation
Peak aircraft over a community divided by what D permits a tile at that ambient level to hold, averaged over the tiles in the tier that carried traffic. 1.00 means the cap is exactly binding; a blank tier carried nothing.
Tile capacity
How many simultaneous overflights the row's own D actually permits at 45 / 55 / 65 dBA. Analytic, not measured — it follows from the fact that noise adds in energy.
Peak added
Same quantity as Peak dB: the worst added level any single community suffers at any timestep.

Experiment 4

Solver cost: the tractable principles are not the intuitive ones

What does each principle cost to compute, and how far up the fleet ladder can it be solved to proven optimality at all?

Setup. Wall time to a proven optimum, eight solves at a time on 14 cores. No time budget, so a cell that has not returned is genuinely hard rather than merely cut off.

The four conditions expressible as hard caps prove out across the whole ladder, from about two seconds at N=6 to between 231 and 696 seconds at N=32, never more than a factor of 3.1 apart. The two expressed as optimisation objectives over a decibel-valued sum are in a different complexity regime entirely, and no budget fixes it.

Utilitarian proves at N=6 in 77 s and N=8 in 329 s. Proportional proves the same two sizes in 4583 s and 29395 s — 59× and 89× Utilitarian’s time for the identical fleet, so the penalty for pricing the burden per community rather than summing it is itself growing with N.

Experiments 5 and 6

What moves a metric the ladder leaves flat

Travel time is identical across every principle at every fleet size. Is that a property of the principles, or of a setup that gives none of them anywhere to go?

Setup. Two knobs, each acting on a different half of the menu. Horizon slack widens T_max from the Chebyshev floor +1 that the tool sends, giving an aircraft room to detour into. Cap tightness lowers D until it binds, so routing around a full community becomes the only option. Unlimited budget on both, so a flat line means the principle declined the room rather than ran out of clock.

What the columns mean

Condition
Which of the six payloads was solved — one of the five fairness principles, or Baseline: the same fleet with both caps opened to 30 dB and every objective switched off, i.e. the shortest-time routing the solver returns when no principle has been chosen.
N
Fleet size — how many aircraft are in the air, each flying one origin–destination trip between two of the three vertiports.
Avg hops
Mean trip length in timesteps, counted from an aircraft's first move to its first arrival. One timestep is 180 s, so 2.75 hops is about 8½ minutes aloft.
vs base
Total fleet hops above the Baseline row at the same N. This is the travel-time price of the principle. Zero means it cost nothing.
Max/tile
The largest number of aircraft over a single community at a single timestep — the concentration the caps exist to limit.
Shared
Tile-timesteps carrying two or more aircraft at once. A community overflown twice in one timestep contributes one.
Total dB
Added noise summed over every community and every timestep. This is exactly the quantity the Utilitarian objective minimises. It is an arithmetic sum of decibels, so it is an index rather than a level anyone hears.
Peak dB
The worst added level any one community suffers at any one timestep — the quantity the cap D bounds, and the number a resident of the loudest-hit community would experience.
45 dBA share
Percentage of the fleet's total flight time spent over the quietest tier of communities. It falls when a principle pushes traffic onto already-loud tiles.
Wall
Seconds of solver time to reach and prove the optimum, with eight solves running at once. Comparable within this sweep only.
Status
optimal means proven best for that objective — not merely the best found before a clock ran out. A cell still searching shows how long it has run instead.

Where this comes from

  • Figures — paper/tex/figs/*.pdf (PNG twins alongside), written by harness/figures.py
  • Every number — harness/results/fleet_metrics.csv, one row per solve
  • Prose with row keys — harness/results/fleet_findings.md
  • What ran, and what broke — harness/NIGHT_REPORT.md
  • Judgement calls — harness/DECISIONS.md
